name: Appeal to Ignorance
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Treating a claim as true because it has not been disproved, or false because it has not been proved.
better_move: Ask what evidence actually supports the claim. Lack of disproof is not proof.
examples: “You must be hiding something because I cannot prove that you are not.”
“If you really were not talking to your ex, you should be able to prove every gap in the record.”

name: Shifting the Burden of Proof
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Making a claim and then requiring the other person to disprove it instead of supporting the claim yourself.
better_move: The person making the factual claim should identify the evidence for it.
examples: “You are trying to isolate me.” “What did I do?” “Prove that you are not.”
“You only went to the gym to meet someone.” “What makes you think that?” “Show me that I am wrong.”

name: Demanding Impossible Proof
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Setting a standard of proof that no person could realistically satisfy, especially for private intentions, memories, or hypothetical alternatives.
better_move: Replace impossible certainty with reasonable evidence, observable behavior, and clear future agreements.
examples: “Prove that you never intended to hurt me.”
“Prove that you would have made the same choice if we had never argued.”

name: Appeal to Authority
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Treating an authority figure’s opinion as conclusive proof rather than examining the reasons and evidence behind it.
better_move: Use expertise as input, not as a substitute for reasoning. Ask what the conclusion is based on.
examples: “The therapist said you are avoidant, so every time you ask for space is avoidance.”
“My family says you are controlling, so that settles it.”

name: Appeal to Popularity
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Treating a belief as true because many people agree with it.
better_move: Popularity can reveal norms, but it does not prove what happened or what agreement is right for a particular couple.
examples: “Everyone I told agrees that you were wrong.”
“All my friends think married people should share their location, so you should too.”

name: Anecdotal Fallacy
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Using a small number of personal examples as if they establish a broad rule or pattern.
better_move: Treat examples as data points, then check whether the wider pattern supports the same conclusion.
examples: “The last two times I asked a question you got upset, so I can never ask you anything.”
“You were tired after work three nights this week, so your career always comes before us.”

name: Hasty Generalization
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Drawing a sweeping conclusion from too little or unrepresentative evidence.
better_move: Slow down the leap from one event to a global conclusion. Ask how often, under what conditions, and with what exceptions.
examples: “You forgot one school event, so you are not invested in the family.”
“You changed one agreement, so nothing you say can ever be trusted.”

name: Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Selecting a cluster of events that fit a story while ignoring the larger set of events that do not fit it.
better_move: Define the pattern first, then examine all relevant cases instead of drawing the target around the cases that fit.
examples: Four arguments happened after late work shifts, so only those four are highlighted while calm late-shift nights disappear from the story.
Three examples of a spouse declining affection are grouped together while many accepted hugs are ignored.

name: Cherry-Picking
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Presenting only the evidence that supports a preferred conclusion while omitting relevant evidence that points another way.
better_move: Ask what evidence would complicate the story, not only what evidence confirms it.
examples: Listing every time a partner was unavailable while leaving out the times they rearranged work to be present.
Citing one text that sounds romantic while omitting the surrounding exchange that changes its meaning.

name: False Cause
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Assuming that because two things occur together or in sequence, one caused the other without enough evidence.
better_move: Separate sequence from causation. Look for alternative causes, repeated patterns, and direct mechanisms.
examples: “We started arguing after you joined the gym, therefore the gym caused our problems.”
“You became distant after your schedule changed, so your job must be the reason you stopped loving me.”

name: Illusory Correlation
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Perceiving a connection between two things more strongly than the evidence supports.
better_move: Track whether the connection actually occurs consistently rather than relying on how strongly the association feels.
examples: Believing every unanswered text predicts a later argument because the memorable cases stand out.
Linking every trip to see family with marital distance even though many trips were uneventful.

name: Base-Rate Neglect
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Ignoring the ordinary frequency of an event while focusing on a vivid explanation for a particular case.
better_move: Ask what usually happens in comparable situations before choosing the most threatening explanation.
examples: A late reply is treated as evidence of avoidance without considering how often busy people simply reply late.
A change in sexual desire is treated as proof of lost love without considering fatigue, stress, medication, health, or conflict.

name: Availability Heuristic
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Judging what is likely or typical by whichever examples come to mind most easily, especially vivid or painful ones.
better_move: Vivid memories deserve attention, but estimate frequency from the whole record, not from the easiest memory to retrieve.
examples: One explosive argument makes it feel as though every disagreement becomes explosive.
A past betrayal makes a present ambiguity feel more likely to be betrayal.

name: Outcome Bias
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Judging the quality of a decision mainly by how it turned out rather than by what was reasonably knowable when the decision was made.
better_move: Evaluate the decision using the information, risks, and alternatives available at the time—not only the ending.
examples: “The trip ended badly, so agreeing to the trip was obviously irresponsible.”
“The dog never bit anyone here, so withholding its history did not matter.”

name: Argument from Repetition
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Treating a claim as more credible simply because it has been repeated many times.
better_move: Repetition can strengthen memory and emotion, but it does not add evidence. Return to the underlying events.
examples: “I have told you for years that you never support me, so it must be true.”
A label such as “controlling” becomes accepted because it is used repeatedly, even when the underlying behaviors are never specified.

name: Proof by Assertion
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Repeating a conclusion confidently as though confidence itself establishes the conclusion.
better_move: Turn the assertion into a testable statement: what observation would support it, and what would count against it?
examples: “You were trying to punish me.” “No.” “Yes, you were.”
“This is what you always do.” When asked for examples, the same sentence is simply repeated.

name: Argument from Silence
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Treating a lack of statement or response as evidence for a particular conclusion when silence could have many meanings.
better_move: Silence is information, but it is ambiguous information. Ask before assigning a single meaning to it.
examples: “You did not say you wanted me, so you must not desire me.”
“You did not defend me in that moment, so you agreed with them.”

name: False Balance
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Treating two sides as equally supported merely because two sides exist.
better_move: Respect both people without pretending all claims have equal evidence. People deserve equal dignity; claims still require evaluation.
examples: One partner produces a dated message and the other says, “That never happened,” and the disagreement is treated as exactly fifty-fifty without examining the record.
A concrete safety concern and a speculative fear are treated as having identical evidentiary weight.

name: Fallacy Fallacy
group_core: Does the evidence actually support the conclusion?
definition: Assuming that because someone used bad reasoning, the conclusion they reached must therefore be false.
better_move: Correct the reasoning without assuming the opposite conclusion. A bad argument can accidentally point toward a true concern.
examples: A spouse catastrophizes about the marriage, so the real relationship problem is dismissed as imaginary.
Someone uses an exaggerated “always,” so every underlying complaint is rejected.

name: Mind Reading
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Assuming you know what another person thinks, feels, or intends without sufficient evidence.
better_move: Replace certainty about motive with a question: “What was happening for you when you did that?”
examples: “You asked where I was going because you do not trust me.”
“You did not initiate sex because you are punishing me.”

name: Jumping to Conclusions
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Moving from limited information to a firm conclusion before enough evidence is available.
better_move: Name the observation first, then list at least two plausible explanations before acting on one.
examples: A wedding ring is missing, so the marriage must be ending.
A spouse wants time alone after work, so they must be emotionally checked out.

name: Appeal to Motive
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Trying to discredit a statement by assigning a questionable motive to the speaker instead of addressing the statement itself.
better_move: A motive may matter, but it does not determine whether the statement is true. Evaluate both separately.
examples: “You only want counseling so you can look like the good spouse.”
“You only apologized because you want sex.”

name: Intentionality Bias
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Assuming that an unwanted outcome was deliberately caused even when accident, habit, stress, or misunderstanding could explain it.
better_move: Distinguish “this affected me” from “you intended this effect.” Ask what evidence establishes intention.
examples: “You forgot to tell me because you wanted me to feel excluded.”
“You came home late because you knew it would upset me.”

name: Hostile Attribution Bias
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Interpreting ambiguous behavior as hostile, disrespectful, or threatening more readily than neutral alternatives.
better_move: When evidence is ambiguous, deliberately generate a neutral explanation before choosing the hostile one.
examples: A short text is read as contempt rather than exhaustion.
A request for space is read as punishment rather than regulation.

name: Personalization
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Taking an event personally or assuming you caused it when many other factors may be involved.
better_move: Ask what portion is actually yours. Responsibility can be partial without being total.
examples: “She is exhausted after a twelve-hour shift, therefore I must be failing as a husband.”
“He is quiet tonight, so I must have done something wrong.”

name: Projection
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Attributing your own feelings, motives, or fears to another person without adequate evidence.
better_move: Use first-person language for your internal state before assigning it to the other person.
examples: Someone who fears abandonment assumes their spouse must secretly be preparing to leave.
A person feeling guilty assumes the other partner is judging them even before anything is said.

name: Genetic Fallacy
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Judging a claim by where it came from rather than by whether the claim is supported.
better_move: The source can affect credibility, but the claim still deserves evaluation on its own merits.
examples: “You only think that because your therapist told you.”
“That boundary came from your family, so it is unhealthy.”

name: Personal Incredulity
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Assuming something cannot be true because you personally cannot understand how it could be true.
better_move: Not understanding another person’s experience is a reason to investigate, not proof that the experience is false.
examples: “I cannot understand how you forgot that conversation, so you must be lying.”
“I would never need that much space from someone I love, so you cannot really love me.”

name: Illusion of Transparency
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Overestimating how obvious your thoughts, needs, or intentions are to another person.
better_move: Say the part you assume is obvious. Relationships fail when invisible intentions are treated as shared information.
examples: “She should know that when I ask questions I am trying to understand, not accuse.”
“He should know I wanted him to initiate without me having to say it.”

name: Curse of Knowledge
group_core: Am I observing intent, or assuming it?
definition: Once you know something, underestimating how difficult it may be for someone else to understand it without your background, context, or assumptions.
better_move: Explain the missing context without assuming that failure to infer it means indifference or bad faith.
examples: A person who knows the full history of a family conflict assumes their spouse should immediately see why a comment is threatening.
Someone familiar with a neighborhood’s risks expects their partner to interpret a late-night location exactly the same way.

name: Emotional Reasoning
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Treating a feeling as proof that the external interpretation attached to that feeling must be true.
better_move: Validate the feeling first, then separately examine the claim about what caused it.
examples: “I feel controlled, therefore you are controlling me.”
“I feel unwanted, therefore you do not desire me.”

name: Appeal to Emotion
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Using fear, guilt, pity, anger, or another emotion to persuade instead of providing reasons for the conclusion.
better_move: Emotion can explain why something matters; it should not replace the reasoning needed to justify a demand or conclusion.
examples: “If you loved me, you would cancel your plans because you can see how upset I am.”
“How can you disagree with me after everything I have suffered?”

name: Appeal to Consequences
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Arguing that a claim must be true or false because accepting it would have desirable or painful consequences.
better_move: Truth is independent of whether the conclusion is comfortable. Separate what is true from what you fear it would mean.
examples: “If I admit I misunderstood you, then my pain would not count, so I could not have misunderstood.”
“If this agreement really was broken, I would have to reconsider the marriage, so it cannot be that serious.”

name: Reification
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Treating an abstract label or concept as though it were a directly observed concrete fact.
better_move: Return from labels to observable behavior: what was said, done, requested, or prevented?
examples: “You asked three questions; that is control.”
“You took space; that is abandonment.”

name: Black-and-White Thinking
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Reducing a complicated situation to two absolute categories with no meaningful middle ground.
better_move: Look for the third position: partial agreement, temporary limits, mixed motives, incremental repair, or uncertainty.
examples: “Either I care intensely or I become numb.”
“Either she gives me what I need or she does not love me.”

name: Catastrophizing
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Treating a possible negative outcome as imminent, inevitable, or unbearable without enough evidence.
better_move: Ask: What is possible? What is probable? What could I cope with if the difficult outcome happened?
examples: “If she needs space tonight, this marriage is probably over.”
“If I do not resolve this before she goes to work, we may never resolve it.”

name: Labeling
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Turning a behavior or event into a fixed identity statement about a person.
better_move: Describe the behavior precisely. Identities are harder to repair than actions.
examples: “You lied once, therefore you are a liar.”
“You became defensive, therefore you are a defensive person.”

name: Should Statements
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Treating personal expectations as universal rules and then using the rule to generate guilt, resentment, or judgment.
better_move: Translate “should” into a preference, value, agreement, or negotiable expectation.
examples: “A wife should know when her husband needs affection.”
“A husband should never need reassurance.”

name: Fortune Telling
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Predicting a future outcome as though it were already known.
better_move: Treat predictions as hypotheses. Ask what evidence would update the prediction.
examples: “If I stop pursuing, she will leave.”
“If we talk about this, it will become another fight.”

name: Framing Effect
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Changing judgment because the same information is presented through a different emotional or verbal frame.
better_move: Translate charged labels back into concrete actions before deciding what the behavior means.
examples: “I need independence” can sound healthy while “I want distance from you” can sound rejecting, even when the practical request is identical.
“Checking on safety” and “tracking” may describe overlapping behavior but produce very different reactions.

name: Spotlight Effect
group_core: Is a feeling being used as proof of an outside fact?
definition: Overestimating how much other people notice, judge, or focus on your behavior.
better_move: Ask what evidence shows that others are actually focused on you as intensely as you imagine.
examples: A spouse assumes everyone at dinner noticed the couple’s tension and judged the marriage.
Someone believes one awkward therapy comment defined the entire session in the therapist’s mind.

name: Recency Bias
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: Giving disproportionate weight to the most recent events when judging a longer pattern.
better_move: Use a wider time window when evaluating patterns.
examples: One bad Friday becomes evidence that the entire month was bad.
Two recent affectionate nights make months of disconnection feel resolved.

name: Negativity Bias
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: Giving negative events more attention and psychological weight than equally real positive events.
better_move: Do not force positivity; simply make sure negative evidence is not the only evidence recorded.
examples: Remembering the argument after dinner more strongly than the enjoyable dinner itself.
A spouse recalls every rejected initiation while barely registering accepted affection.

name: Hindsight Bias
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: After knowing an outcome, believing the outcome was more predictable than it actually was beforehand.
better_move: Reconstruct what you actually knew then, not what seems obvious now.
examples: “I should have known that agreement would fall apart.”
“The warning signs were obvious; I was stupid not to act immediately.”

name: Anchoring
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: Allowing an early number, label, story, or interpretation to exert excessive influence on later judgments.
better_move: Ask whether the anchor still deserves its influence in light of newer information.
examples: The first description of a partner as “controlling” becomes the lens for later questions.
An early promise about where the couple would live becomes the reference point for every later housing discussion.

name: Memory Conformity
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: Allowing another person’s retelling to alter or reshape your own memory of an event.
better_move: Separate what you independently remember from what you later heard or inferred.
examples: After hearing a family member repeatedly describe an argument, a person becomes less sure which details they personally remember.
A couple’s shared story of “the night everything changed” gradually becomes more uniform even though their original accounts differed.

name: Consistency Bias
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: Remembering your past attitudes or behavior as more consistent with your present self than they really were.
better_move: Allow your past self to have been different. Change does not require rewriting the earlier position.
examples: “I have always wanted strong boundaries,” even though the relationship originally had very few.
“I never wanted children,” when the actual position changed several times.

name: Rosy Retrospection
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: Remembering the past as better, simpler, or more harmonious than it actually was.
better_move: Use nostalgia as information about what you miss, not proof that the past was problem-free.
examples: “Before therapy we were natural and everything worked.”
“The beginning of our marriage had no boundaries and therefore no problems.”

name: Fading Affect Bias
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: The tendency for the emotional intensity of unpleasant memories to fade differently from pleasant memories, sometimes changing how the past is judged.
better_move: Remember that emotional intensity changes over time and may change differently for different people.
examples: An old argument is remembered mainly for the factual dispute while the fear or humiliation attached to it has faded.
A past vacation is remembered warmly while the conflict surrounding it becomes less vivid.

name: Halo Effect
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: Allowing one positive quality or impression to make unrelated judgments about a person more favorable.
better_move: Evaluate each behavior on its own evidence rather than borrowing credibility from unrelated strengths.
examples: Because a partner is a devoted professional, their relationship decisions are assumed to be equally thoughtful.
Because someone is a loving parent, it is assumed they could not behave unfairly in conflict.

name: Horn Effect
group_core: Could memory or perception be shaping the story?
definition: Allowing one negative quality or event to contaminate unrelated judgments about the whole person.
better_move: A serious negative event may matter greatly, but do not let it silently become evidence for unrelated claims.
examples: One broken agreement makes every later promise feel worthless.
One harsh argument turns ordinary questions into evidence of hostility.

name: Overgeneralization
group_core: Did a specific event become an absolute story?
definition: Turning a limited event or pattern into an absolute claim, often using words such as always, never, everything, or nothing.
better_move: Replace absolutes with frequency and examples: “This happened three times this month, and it is affecting my trust.”
examples: “You never support me.”
“Every time I ask a question, you call me defensive.”

name: Slippery Slope
group_core: Did a specific event become an absolute story?
definition: Claiming that one step will inevitably trigger a chain of increasingly severe outcomes without enough support for each link.
better_move: Examine each proposed link separately instead of treating the chain as automatic.
examples: “If we sleep separately tonight, soon we will be roommates, then we will divorce.”
“If I stop checking your location, I will miss a danger, then something terrible will happen.”

name: Composition Fallacy
group_core: Did a specific event become an absolute story?
definition: Assuming that what is true of one part must be true of the whole.
better_move: Keep the scale of the conclusion matched to the scale of the evidence.
examples: “You acted selfishly in this decision, therefore you are selfish.”
“This therapy session was unbalanced, therefore the therapist is incapable of balance.”

name: Division Fallacy
group_core: Did a specific event become an absolute story?
definition: Assuming that what is true of the whole must be true of every part.
better_move: Shared systems can contain unequal contributions. Evaluate the specific part instead of inheriting the judgment of the whole.
examples: “Our marriage is unhealthy, so every affectionate moment between us must be unhealthy too.”
“Our family is financially stable, so neither spouse can have a legitimate money concern.”

name: False Analogy
group_core: Did a specific event become an absolute story?
definition: Treating two situations as equivalent because they resemble each other in one respect while ignoring important differences.
better_move: Identify the relevant similarities and the relevant differences before carrying a conclusion from one case to another.
examples: “Asking where I am going is the same as forbidding me to go.”
“Changing your mind about dinner is the same as changing your mind about a major marital agreement.”

name: Maximization
group_core: Did a specific event become an absolute story?
definition: Inflating the importance, frequency, or meaning of a negative event beyond what the evidence supports.
better_move: Use proportionate language. Serious problems do not become more serious by making them larger than the evidence allows.
examples: A tense conversation becomes “the entire weekend was ruined.”
A partner’s hesitation becomes “you rejected me completely.”

name: Minimization
group_core: Did a specific event become an absolute story?
definition: Reducing the importance or impact of an event in order to make it easier to dismiss.
better_move: Describe the event accurately enough to capture both behavior and impact without exaggerating or shrinking it.
examples: “It was only yelling.”
“It was just a text with an ex.”

name: False Consensus Effect
group_core: Did a specific event become an absolute story?
definition: Overestimating how many reasonable people share your assumptions, values, or preferred rules.
better_move: Your norm may be common, uncommon, or somewhere between. A couple still has to make its own explicit agreements.
examples: “Any husband would be upset by that.”
“Everyone knows spouses should share passwords.”

name: No True Scotsman
group_core: Did a specific event become an absolute story?
definition: Protecting a general rule by redefining the category whenever a counterexample appears.
better_move: Let counterexamples test the rule instead of changing the definition to save the rule.
examples: “A real husband would always want sex.” When a loving husband has low desire: “Then he is not acting like a real husband.”
“A supportive spouse never questions career decisions.” Any questioning spouse is then defined as unsupportive.

name: Ad Hominem
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Attacking the person instead of addressing the claim or behavior being discussed.
better_move: Return to the proposition: even an imperfect messenger can raise a legitimate issue.
examples: “You said you would be home at eight.” “You are impossible to live with.”
“Can we talk about the broken agreement?” “You are obsessed with being right.”

name: Loaded Question
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Asking a question that smuggles in an unproven assumption.
better_move: Remove the assumption and ask the observable question first.
examples: “Why do you keep trying to control me?”
“When are you going to stop choosing your job over this marriage?”

name: Begging the Question
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Assuming the conclusion inside the reasoning that is supposed to prove it.
better_move: Supply independent reasons instead of restating the conclusion in new words.
examples: “Why is that controlling?” “Because it is controlling behavior.”
“How do you know I do not care?” “Because you are uncaring.”

name: Motte-and-Bailey
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Making a strong, controversial claim, then retreating to a weaker, easier-to-defend claim when challenged, while later returning to the stronger one.
better_move: Keep the claim at one level. A feeling of being unsupported may be valid without proving prohibition or deliberate isolation.
examples: “You do not let me have friends.” When challenged: “I only mean I do not feel supported socially.” Later the original claim returns unchanged.
“You never care about my work.” When examples appear: “I mean you do not always understand how tired I am.”

name: Equivocation
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Using the same word in different senses during one argument and treating the meanings as interchangeable.
better_move: Define the key word. Many circular fights are really fights between different definitions.
examples: “Freedom” means being physically allowed to go in one sentence and being emotionally free from disapproval in the next.
“Support” shifts between doing chores, agreeing with decisions, and never criticizing work choices.

name: Moving the Goalposts
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Changing the standard for success after the original standard has been met.
better_move: Before evaluating success, state what would count as meeting the request and do not silently replace it afterward.
examples: “I need you to help more.” Help increases. “I should not have had to ask.”
“I need an apology.” The apology comes. “If you were truly sorry, I would not still be hurt.”

name: Red Herring
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Introducing a different issue that distracts from the issue currently being examined.
better_move: Park the second issue and return to it after the first question is answered.
examples: “You said you would tell me if the plan changed.” “Well, you went through my phone years ago.”
“Why did you yell?” “What about how little sex we have?”

name: Whataboutism
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Responding to criticism by pointing to another person’s wrongdoing rather than addressing the original behavior.
better_move: Two wrongs can both deserve attention. Address them one at a time.
examples: “You yelled at me last night.” “What about when you yelled last month?”
“I need you to keep this agreement.” “What about the promise you broke three years ago?”

name: Tu Quoque
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Rejecting a criticism because the critic has behaved similarly, as though hypocrisy makes the criticism false.
better_move: A person can be inconsistent and still make a valid point. Deal with the behavior, then deal with the hypocrisy separately.
examples: “You should not interrupt me.” “You interrupt me too.”
“We should not discuss our marriage with family.” “You talked to the kids before.”

name: Poisoning the Well
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Discrediting a person in advance so that whatever they say will be interpreted through a negative label.
better_move: Evaluate the statement before using a character judgment to decide what it means.
examples: “He is extremely defensive, so expect him to deny everything.”
“She is avoidant, so anything she says about needing space is just avoidance.”

name: Appeal to Ridicule
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Mocking a position instead of showing why it is wrong.
better_move: A position can sound awkward and still be reasonable. Critique the substance, not how easy it is to mock.
examples: “You need a scheduled time to talk? That sounds like a business meeting, not a marriage.”
“You want consent to be explicit? How romantic.”

name: Appeal to Tradition
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Treating an established practice as correct merely because it has been done that way before.
better_move: Tradition can carry meaning, but current conditions still determine whether the practice works.
examples: “We never had boundaries when we started dating, so we should not need them now.”
“I have always handled the finances, so there is no reason to change.”

name: Appeal to Novelty
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Treating a new approach as superior simply because it is new.
better_move: Newness is neither proof of improvement nor proof of decline. Evaluate results and principles.
examples: “Relationship 2.0 is new, so it must be healthier than what we had.”
“This new therapy language is more evolved, so ordinary direct speech is inferior.”

name: Appeal to Nature
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Treating something as good, right, or unavoidable simply because it is described as natural.
better_move: Natural impulses still operate inside consent, responsibility, and negotiated agreements.
examples: “Jealousy is natural, so checking a partner’s phone is justified.”
“Sex is natural in marriage, so a spouse should provide it.”

name: Straw Man
group_core: Are we still answering the original question?
definition: Distorting another person’s position into a more extreme or simpler claim that is easier to attack.
better_move: Restate the other person’s actual claim in a form they recognize before responding to it.
examples: “I want us to discuss major purchases.” “So I need permission to spend any money?”
“I need clarity about what happened.” “So feelings mean nothing to you?”

name: False Equivalence
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Treating two things as equally significant because they share a superficial similarity while ignoring relevant differences.
better_move: Compare the features that actually matter: consent, frequency, stakes, intent, impact, and prior agreement.
examples: Changing dinner plans is treated as equivalent to reversing a major pre-marital agreement.
Looking at a phone after being invited to retrieve something is treated as identical to secretly monitoring a device for weeks.

name: Special Pleading
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Creating an exception for yourself or your preferred case without a relevant reason for why the ordinary standard should not apply.
better_move: If an exception is justified, name the relevant difference. Otherwise apply the same rule.
examples: “You should not discuss our relationship with other people, but I needed to talk to my family.”
“You must keep agreements, but this agreement should not count because my feelings changed.”

name: Double Standard
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Judging substantially similar behavior differently depending on who does it.
better_move: Ask whether you would accept the same standard with the roles reversed.
examples: One spouse’s questions are called curiosity while the other’s are called interrogation.
One partner may change plans without explanation while the other is criticized for unpredictability.

name: Selective Accountability
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Demanding responsibility for one person’s contribution while excluding another person’s relevant contribution from examination.
better_move: Accountability is not fifty-fifty in every event, but every relevant behavior should be examinable.
examples: Only the reaction is discussed while the behavior that preceded it is declared off-limits.
Only the broken privacy boundary is discussed while the content discovered is treated as irrelevant.

name: Fundamental Attribution Error
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Explaining another person’s behavior mainly through character while underestimating situational pressures.
better_move: Consider both disposition and situation before turning behavior into character.
examples: “You asked ten questions because you are controlling,” rather than considering fear, uncertainty, or a need for clarity.
“You did not want sex because you are cold,” rather than considering exhaustion or unresolved conflict.

name: Actor-Observer Bias
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Explaining your own behavior through circumstances while explaining another person’s behavior through personality.
better_move: Describe both people with the same level of situational generosity and behavioral accountability.
examples: “I raised my voice because I was overwhelmed; you raised yours because you are disrespectful.”
“I needed space because I was exhausted; you needed space because you are avoidant.”

name: Self-Serving Bias
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Interpreting successes in ways that credit yourself and failures in ways that protect yourself from responsibility.
better_move: Use the same causal standard for outcomes that flatter you and outcomes that do not.
examples: “The good week happened because I changed; the bad argument happened because you triggered me.”
“The children are doing well because of my parenting; their distress comes from your influence.”

name: Self-Justification
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Constructing reasons after the fact that make your behavior feel necessary, reasonable, or inevitable.
better_move: An explanation can be true and still not eliminate responsibility. Ask what alternative choices existed.
examples: “I had to keep asking because you would not give me clarity.”
“I had to withdraw because you would not stop asking.”

name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Continuing a course mainly because of what has already been invested, even when future costs and benefits point elsewhere.
better_move: Past investment matters emotionally, but the decision should turn on future values, costs, and possibilities.
examples: “We have spent ten years together, so leaving would waste those years.”
“We have already paid for months of therapy, so we have to keep going.”

name: Moral Licensing
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Using a previous good deed or sacrifice as permission to behave less responsibly afterward.
better_move: Good actions do not purchase exemptions from consent, accountability, or respect.
examples: “I do everything around the house, so I am entitled to push for sex.”
“I moved for this marriage, so I should get the final say on where we live next.”

name: Just-World Fallacy
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Assuming people generally get outcomes they deserve, which can lead to blaming someone for harm simply because the harm occurred.
better_move: Bad outcomes can arise from mixed causes, incompatible needs, chance, trauma, or another person’s choices.
examples: “If your previous marriage failed, you must have caused it somehow.”
“If someone feels isolated, their spouse must have isolated them.”

name: Zero-Sum Thinking
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Assuming that one person’s gain must be the other person’s loss when cooperative outcomes may exist.
better_move: Look for arrangements where both needs can be represented, even if neither gets everything.
examples: “If your career gets what it needs, the marriage necessarily loses.”
“If I honor your boundary, my needs no longer matter.”

name: Omission Bias
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Judging harmful action more strongly than harmful inaction, or treating inaction as morally neutral when it can also have consequences.
better_move: Ask what responsibility attaches both to what was done and to what was knowingly left undone.
examples: Breaking a promise is condemned while repeatedly refusing to revisit an unworkable promise is treated as doing nothing.
Yelling is recognized as harmful while silently withholding critical safety information is treated as less significant because it involved no overt act.

name: Moral Luck
group_core: Would the same rule seem fair if the roles were reversed?
definition: Judging someone’s moral responsibility mainly by outcomes that were partly outside their control rather than by the quality of the choice itself.
better_move: Separate the controllable choice from the uncontrollable outcome when assigning responsibility.
examples: A risky decision is treated as harmless because nothing bad happened.
A reasonable safety decision is treated as foolish because the outcome happened to be bad.

name: Confirmation Bias
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Seeking, noticing, interpreting, and remembering information in ways that support an existing belief while discounting contrary evidence.
better_move: Actively search for the strongest evidence against your preferred conclusion.
examples: Once someone believes “my partner does not care,” every missed bid is noticed and every act of care is explained away.
Once someone believes “my spouse is controlling,” ordinary questions are interpreted through that lens.

name: Belief Perseverance
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Continuing to hold a belief even after the evidence that originally supported it has weakened or been corrected.
better_move: When the foundation changes, deliberately reconsider the conclusion rather than merely finding a new justification for it.
examples: A spouse remains convinced that a partner opposed all friendships even after acknowledging no friendship was actually prohibited.
A person keeps believing an agreement was never discussed even after messages show that it was.

name: Backfire Effect
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: A pattern in which corrective information can sometimes cause a person to defend an existing belief more strongly instead of updating it.
better_move: Lower the identity threat. Ask what part of the belief can be updated without erasing the underlying experience.
examples: Evidence that contradicts a painful story leads to even stronger insistence that the story must be true.
A calm correction is experienced as proof that the other person is “lawyering” the conversation.

name: Naive Realism
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Assuming that you see reality objectively and that people who disagree must be uninformed, irrational, or biased.
better_move: Separate confidence in evidence from the assumption that your interpretation is the only reasonable one.
examples: “I am simply being logical; if you disagree you are being emotional.”
“I know what happened, so anyone who interprets it differently is rewriting reality.”

name: Bias Blind Spot
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Seeing cognitive biases readily in other people while underestimating your own susceptibility to them.
better_move: Before naming another person’s reasoning error, ask where the same category might appear in your own thinking.
examples: A person can name a partner’s emotional reasoning but miss their own catastrophizing.
Someone spots the other spouse’s confirmation bias while selectively collecting evidence of that bias.

name: Kafka Trap
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Treating denial of an accusation as evidence that the accusation is true, making the claim impossible to challenge.
better_move: A fair claim must allow some possible response or evidence that could count against it.
examples: “You are defensive.” “I disagree.” “See? That defensiveness proves it.”
“You are controlling.” “What behavior are you referring to?” “Needing evidence is part of your control.”

name: False Dilemma
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Presenting only two options when additional possibilities exist.
better_move: List at least one third option before accepting an either-or frame.
examples: “Either you trust me completely or you do not trust me at all.”
“Either I pursue closeness or I stop caring.”

name: Circular Reasoning
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Using the conclusion as its own support so that the argument never reaches independent evidence.
better_move: Break the circle by asking for an observation that can be evaluated independently of the conclusion.
examples: “You are selfish because you only think about yourself; I know you only think about yourself because you are selfish.”
“This relationship is unsafe because I feel unsafe; I know my feeling proves danger because the relationship is unsafe.”

name: Status Quo Bias
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Preferring the current arrangement mainly because it is familiar, even when alternatives may better fit present needs.
better_move: Compare the current arrangement with realistic alternatives instead of treating familiarity as evidence of superiority.
examples: Keeping the same living arrangement because changing it feels more threatening than examining whether it works.
Avoiding new boundaries because the relationship began without them.

name: Reactance
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Resisting a request or idea partly because it feels like a threat to autonomy, even when the idea itself may be reasonable.
better_move: Notice the autonomy alarm, then evaluate the request separately from the discomfort of being asked.
examples: A spouse becomes more determined to go somewhere simply because their partner strongly asks them not to.
A person rejects a useful communication technique because it feels imposed by therapy.

don’t tell me what to do

name: In-Group Bias
group_core: What evidence could change my mind?
definition: Giving more trust, generosity, or credibility to people perceived as belonging to your group than to outsiders.
better_move: Apply the same evidence standard to insiders and outsiders.
examples: A spouse automatically trusts their family’s account of the marriage over the partner’s account.
Friends’ interpretations are treated as neutral while the spouse’s are treated as self-serving.
